name: Naltrexone
route_note: Oral tablets daily; extended-release IM microsphere injection every 4 weeks.

discovery.note: Synthesised from thebaine/oxymorphone as a longer-acting, orally active successor to naloxone; development was later supported by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse.

tagline: Long-acting opioid antagonist for alcohol and opioid use disorders
summary: Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid receptor antagonist used to support abstinence in opioid use disorder after detoxification and to reduce heavy drinking in alcohol use disorder. It is available as a daily tablet and a monthly injection, and in combination with bupropion for weight management.
mechanism: Naltrexone competitively blocks mu-opioid receptors (and, to a lesser extent, kappa and delta receptors), preventing the euphoric and respiratory effects of opioids taken afterwards. Because it can precipitate acute withdrawal, patients must be opioid-free before starting.

In alcohol use disorder, blocking endogenous opioid signalling is thought to reduce alcohol-induced dopamine release in the mesolimbic reward pathway, diminishing the rewarding effects of drinking and craving.
uses: Prevention of relapse to opioid dependence after detoxification

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Naltrexone is approved for opioid dependence (Trexan, DuPont).

history.title: Alcohol trials
history.detail: Volpicelli and O'Malley publish trials showing naltrexone reduces relapse in alcohol dependence.

history.title: Alcohol indication
history.detail: The FDA approves naltrexone (ReVia) for alcohol dependence.

history.title: Vivitrol
history.detail: Monthly extended-release injectable naltrexone is approved for alcohol dependence.

history.title: Opioid indication
history.detail: Vivitrol is approved for prevention of relapse to opioid dependence.

history.title: Boxed warning removed
history.detail: The FDA removes the hepatotoxicity boxed warning from naltrexone labelling.

history.title: Contrave
history.detail: Naltrexone–bupropion is approved for chronic weight management.

pk.metabolism: Hepatic dihydrodiol dehydrogenase to active 6-beta-naltrexol (not CYP)

serious: Opioid overdose after stopping (loss of tolerance)

facts: The X:BOT trial (2017) found that once started, extended-release naltrexone and buprenorphine–naloxone had similar effectiveness for opioid use disorder.
